interest: For historians, this file provides a valuable window into U.S.–Japan cultural diplomacy and public memory during the interwar 1930s, showing how historical ties were commemorated even amidst an increasingly strained geopolitical climate. It offers unique insights into the intersection of diplomacy, religion, and Japanese popular culture, notably in reports detailing the widespread theatrical, cinematic, and shrine adaptations of the Townsend Harris and Okichi legend. Additionally, the collection documents the physical preservation and contestation of material culture—such as custody disputes and temple presentations of Perry and Harris relics—as well as the personal, bilateral connections sustained through direct outreach to General Grant's living descendants.
overview: This file comprises U.S. State Department records (decimal file 894.413) from the 1930s concerning the erection, dedication, custody, and diplomatic commemoration of monuments, statues, and memorials in Japan honoring prominent Americans. Consisting of 30 documents across 88 pages—including diplomatic despatches, internal Division of Far Eastern Affairs memoranda, letters, press releases, transmittals, and photographs—the collection primarily focuses on memorials dedicated to Townsend Harris (at Jigan-in in Kawazu and Zempukuji in Tokyo, alongside relics at Ryosenji in Shimoda), inventor Thomas Alva Edison (at Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine in Yawata), General Ulysses S. Grant (monument and memorial trees in Ueno Park, Tokyo), and anthropologist Dr. Frederick Starr. The records trace American diplomatic engagement led by figures such as Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville, document the popular Japanese cultural reception of historical figures (including the theatrical and cinematic folklore surrounding Harris and Okichi), and detail the distribution of commemorative pamphlets, postcards, and relics to educational institutions and Grant's descendants.
